validity.researcher_notes: EXISTENCE: unambiguously real and well documented across multiple independent origins — Wikipedia, offshore-technology.com (formerly hydrocarbons-technology.com; both a general project page and a page specifically for 'Central Asia–China Line B (Kazakhstan Section)'), the Lowy Institute, and two AidData (William & Mary) project records built from the underlying syndicated-loan documentation. CLASSIFICATION: correctly 'transmission' — this is the major Turkmenistan–Uzbekistan–Kazakhstan–China trunk export system, not a gathering/feeder line. DUPLICATE (the roster's structural flag): checked directly and REFUTED for this row. P2300 (Line B) is NOT the same physical pipe as P2299 (Line A) or P1124 (Line C) — it is a genuinely separate, separately-built, separately-commissioned parallel pipeline. offshore-technology.com's project page lists Line A (completed Dec 2009) and Line B (operational Oct 2010) as two distinct pipes that happen to share the identical 1,833 km route length and 1,067mm/42in diameter because they run side-by-side on the same corridor — the repeated '1,833.00 km' across P2299/P2300 in the roster is the CORRECT shared value, not a copy-paste error. This is independently corroborated at finer grain by AidData project #54489 (built from the CDB/China-financed loan documents for the Kazakh section): 'Lines A and B each measure 1300 km in length' running parallel 'from Shymkent to the Alataw Pass' in southern Kazakhstan, with combined Line A+Line B capacity of 30 bcm/y reached by Oct 20, 2012 — exactly matching GEM's 15.00 bcm/y x 2 (P2299+P2300) split. Line C (P1124) is a later, separately-negotiated third line (CNPC-Uzbekneftegaz agreement Sept 2011, ~2014 completion, 25 bcm/y) — confirmed as a distinct physical asset, not a duplicate of P2300. One out-of-scope note for a future P1124 check: Wikipedia states the diameter of 'each' of Lines A, B and C is 1,067mm/42in, which would conflict with GEM's own P1124 diameter of 1,219mm — flagging for the record since the roster raised it, but it is not this row's defect. FUEL SOURCE caveat: Wikipedia attributes the Galkynysh field specifically to Line D's supply (via Kyrgyzstan/Tajikistan) and names Bagtyyarlyk (at Saman-Depe) plus Iolotan/Sag Kenar as the Lines A/B/C source fields; Jamestown's 2010 analysis separately ties both Dauletabad and Bagtyarlik to the China-bound export system (noting Dauletabad 'had until now been dedicated to exports northward to Russia', i.e. only recently redirected to this pipeline). GEM's three-field FuelSource list for P2300 is plausible and broadly corroborated but not confirmed by one single authoritative per-line source — treat as medium confidence, not a concern. OPERATOR caveat: GEM lists 'Turkmengaz, Uztransgaz, Intergas Central Asia'. Intergas Central Asia's own site confirms it operates Kazakhstan's main gas pipeline system generally, but two independent AidData project pages (built from the actual JV/loan documents) identify the entity specifically chartered to construct, finance AND operate the Kazakh section of this pipeline as 'Asian Gas Pipeline LLP' (AGP), a 50/50 JV of KazTransGas and CNPC (via its subsidiary Trans-Asia Gas Pipeline Co. Ltd) — not Intergas Central Asia by name. This may just be a level-of-detail gap (AGP as legal JV vs. Intergas as the domestic O&M arm under an operating agreement) rather than an error, so flagged as a caveat for Update rather than a hard concern.

fills.researcher_notes: Line B (Kazakhstan Section) 'started operations in 2010' per offshore-technology.com's dedicated marketdata entry; Wikipedia corroborates 'the second line was completed by the end of 2010' and describes both lines as in service today (2022 EIA/Xinhua throughput data cited on the wiki page confirm ongoing operation). Two independent origins, both content-verified.
Both sources describe this uniformly as a natural gas pipeline carrying gas from Turkmen/Uzbek fields to China; not in dispute.
Described consistently across sources as a major cross-border trunk export system (Turkmenistan through Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan to China), i.e. transmission, not a gathering/process line.

offshore-technology.com's Kazakhstan-section-specific page: Line B 'started operations in 2010' (elsewhere dated to 18 Oct 2010 state-acceptance). Wikipedia independently: 'the second line was completed by the end of 2010'. Not filling StartMonth1 (October) since no source gave an exact day/month I could independently corroborate to 2 sources — left blank rather than force it.

No source gives Line B's capacity in isolation; both cited sources give the combined Line A + Line B design capacity as 30 bcm/y (AidData #54489: 'transmit 30 billion cubic meters of natural gas annually' once all A+B compressor stations were operational by Oct 20 2012; offshore-technology.com: overall 'Capacity: 30 bcm/a'). Since Lines A and B are built as identical twin parallel pipes (same length, same diameter, same era) the even 15+15 split matches every source describing them as equal parallel lines; a third source (China AidData #91917, Uzbek section) independently states the same 30 bcm/a combined figure was reached by end 2011. Tier kept at 'high' on the combined figure; the even-split inference to 15.00 for this specific row is reasonable but not itself independently stated anywhere, so flagging that nuance rather than treating 15.00 as directly sourced.

offshore-technology.com states Line B length explicitly as '1,833 km' (same as Line A). Wikipedia: 'The length of Lines A, B, and C is about 1,833 kilometres'. This is the full Gedaim (Turkmenistan/Uzbekistan border) to Horgos (China) route length, consistent with GEM's own StartLocation/EndLocation for this row (Getaim→Horgos) — i.e. this row tracks the whole multi-country line, so the length is correctly the whole-route figure, not a Kazakhstan-only segment length. (The Kazakh segment alone is ~1,300–1,305 km per AidData #54489 and offshore-technology.com's marketdata page — consistent breakdown, not a conflict.)

offshore-technology.com's Kazakhstan-section page: 'maximum diameter of 42 inches'. Wikipedia: 'The diameter of each pipeline is 1,067 millimetres (42.0 in)'. 42in = 1,066.8mm ≈ 1,067mm, so DiameterUnits='in' is correct as-is (not a units error).

Bagtyyarlyk is firmly confirmed as the pipeline's origin field (Wikipedia: 'starts in Saman-Depe carrying natural gas from the Bagtyyarlyk gas fields'; Jamestown: 'newly opened Turkmen fields (Bagtyarlik, dedicated to China)'). Dauletabad is corroborated by Jamestown as feeding this export route (though it notes the field 'had until now been dedicated to exports northward to Russia', i.e. a relatively recent redirection). Galkynysh is the one soft spot: Wikipedia ties Galkynysh specifically to Line D's supply (via Kyrgyzstan/Tajikistan), not explicitly to Lines A/B/C — other secondary aggregations do list Galkynysh among Lines A/B/C's sources, but I could not pin that to one authoritative per-line-specific source. Kept at tier=medium and flagged the Galkynysh nuance rather than asserting it is wrong; not material enough to be a spec concern given the field genuinely feeds the same broader Amu Darya-basin export system.

Intergas Central Asia's own site confirms its role operating Kazakhstan's main gas pipeline system; Wikipedia's partner list (CNPC, Turkmengaz, Uzbekneftegas, KazMunayGas) supports Turkmengaz/Uzbek-side involvement at the national-company level (GEM's 'Uztransgaz' is Uzbekneftegaz's gas-transport subsidiary, a defensible near-match, not necessarily an error). Flagged in the validity section: the JV specifically chartered to build/finance/OPERATE the Kazakh segment of THIS pipeline is 'Asian Gas Pipeline LLP' (AGP, KazTransGas+CNPC 50/50) per two independent AidData records, and it does not appear in GEM's Operator list at all — recommend Update review whether AGP should be added. Kept tier at medium because of that gap; did not overwrite the existing value.

AidData #54489 (from the underlying loan/JV documents): 'KazTransGas and CNPC each hold a 50% equity stake in AGP' for the Kazakh segment — QazaqGaz is KazTransGas's parent national company, and PipeChina is CNPC's post-2019 pipeline-asset spin-off (consistent with the wiki-cited 2020 PetroChina 'Pipeline Restructuring Transactions' presentation), so Owner1/Owner4 line up. Wikipedia independently: pipeline 'partners include China National Petroleum Corporation, Turkmengaz, Uzbekneftegas, and KazMunayGas' — covers Owner2 (Turkmengaz) at the whole-line level; Owner3 'Uztransgaz' is Uzbekneftegaz's transport subsidiary rather than the parent company named by Wikipedia, a minor naming-level nuance, not a materially different entity.

The existing current_ref (thepeoplesmap.net) is live (HTTP 200) but is a JS-rendered page — a plain-text fetch (url_verifier) and a bot-blocked WebFetch (403) both failed to surface 'Getaim'/'Horgos' even though the page is reachable, so its content could not be positively confirmed; per standing rules a live-but-unverifiable page is NOT deleted, only supplemented. Adding offshore-technology.com's project page as a second, fully content-verified ref: 'begins at Gedaim, on the Turkmenistan / Uzbekistan border, and ends at Horgos, in the Xinjiang region of China' — matches every Location field value on this row exactly.

summary: P2300 (Central Asia–China Gas Pipeline, Line B): confirmed real, correctly classified as transmission, and NOT a duplicate of P2299 (Line A) or P1124 (Line C) — the shared 1,833 km length is the corroborated true route length for both twin lines A and B (AidData: ~1,300km Kazakh segment each, Shymkent→Alataw Pass, 30 bcm/y combined). Added high/medium-tier refs (offshore-technology.com, Wikipedia, Lowy Institute, 2x AidData, Jamestown, intergas.kz) for all 9 MISSING_REF cells (Status/Fuel/PipelineType/Start/Capacity/Length/Diameter/FuelSource/Operator/Owner) plus a supplemental Location ref; no UNRESOLVED. Two caveats for Update, not concerns: Operator may be missing 'Asian Gas Pipeline (AGP)' (the actual KZ-segment JV), and FuelSource's 'Galkynysh' is more directly tied by Wikipedia to Line D than to Lines A/B/C.
